content: Portulaca oleracea, commonly referred to as Common Purslane, Verdolaga, Pigweed, Little Hogweed, or Pusley, is an annual succulent plant belonging to the family Portulacaceae. It can grow up to 40 cm in height. This plant is native to India and the Middle East but has become naturalized in various other regions. In some areas, it is considered an invasive weed. However, evidence from Crawford Lake deposits in Ontario suggests that this species was present in North America as early as 1430-1489, indicating its arrival in the pre-Columbian era. The plant is characterized by smooth, reddish stems that are mostly prostrate, with alternate leaves that cluster at the joints and ends of the stems. These flowers begin to bloom in late spring and continue until mid-fall. They open individually at the center of the leaf clusters, but only for a few hours during sunny mornings. The seeds of the plant are produced in small pods that open when the seeds are mature. Purslane has a taproot system with fibrous secondary roots, which allows it to thrive in poor, compacted soils and withstand drought conditions. Culinary Usage Although purslane is often regarded as a weed in the United States, it is widely consumed as a leafy vegetable in many parts of Europe and Asia. It has a slightly sour and salty flavor and can be eaten raw in salads or cooked similarly to spinach. Due to its mucilaginous texture, it is also suitable for use in soups and stews. Australian Aborigines historically used the seeds of purslane to make seedcakes. Nutritionally, purslane is notable for its exceptionally high content of Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). According to Simopoulos, purslane contains 0.1 mg/g of EPA, which is an extraordinary concentration for a land-based vegetable source. EPA is an Omega-3 fatty acid typically found in fish and certain algae. In addition to Omega-3s, purslane is rich in vitamins, particularly vitamin C, some B vitamins, and carotenoids. It also provides essential dietary minerals, including magnesium, calcium, potassium, and iron. The plant contains two types of betalain alkaloid pigments: betacyanins, which give the stems their reddish coloration, and betaxanthins, which contribute to the yellowish hue of the flowers and leaves. Both types of pigments are powerful antioxidants and have demonstrated antimutagenic properties in laboratory studies. Medicinal Usage In traditional Greek medicine, purslane has been used as a treatment for constipation and inflammation of the urinary system. In ancient times, the plant was believed to possess such reliable healing properties that Pliny the Elder recommended wearing it as an amulet to ward off evil influences, as documented in his work Natural History (20.120). Historical Context Purslane has been widely utilized in Greece, with archaeobotanical evidence of its use found at numerous prehistoric sites. In historical contexts, seeds of the plant have been discovered in a protogeometric layer at Kastanas and in the Samian Heraion, dating back to the 7th century BCE. Theophrastus, writing in the 4th century BCE, referred to purslane (known as andrákhne) as one of the summer pot herbs that should be sown in April (Historia Plantarum 7.12). In North India, purslane is known as Sanhti or Punarva and is traditionally used as a liver tonic. It is believed to be beneficial in the treatment of liver diseases.
